A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their full text, equations, figures, and appendices support comparison. Appendix renumbering and relocated material can be matched, and visual inspection resolves extraction limitations.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic experiments in Section 6 and Appendix D, plus CQR and CMR experiments on MEPS data in Appendix E.

after.justification: v2 retains original synthetic results and reports additional optimizer, model, loss-function, data-allocation, and feature-distribution experiments in Appendices C and D.

M1.justification: The core CQR/CMR algorithms, scores, and calibration procedures are retained. v2 adds evaluated adaptations using L1 regularization, a Huber penalty, and two- or three-layer ReLU regressors (Appendices C.5 and D.2.3). These change training objectives or architectures within the existing framework.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates synthetic data and MEPS 19/20. v2 adds abalone, cpusmall, and California Housing, substantially broadening regression domains, and introduces a synthetic scenario with nonlinear conditional quantiles. Figure 12 visibly evaluates neural networks on the three added datasets; its caption also names MEPS, but those panels are absent.

E2.justification: v1's empirical evaluations use SGD without optimizer comparisons. v2 Figure 11 compares SGD with SGDM, Adam, and AdamW, including on retained MEPS datasets. Figure 12 additionally compares linear regressors with two- and three-layer neural networks. These are new evaluated comparator sets.

E3.justification: The original Section 6 settings are retained. New protocols vary optimizers, losses, and network configurations; Appendix D.3 sweeps training fractions from 0.01 to 0.99 with complementary calibration fractions and alpha from 0.001 to 0.2, measuring interval length. Appendix D.2.1 also revises the calibration-share description, although its precise split handling remains ambiguous.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's scaling checks, v2 tests whether phase-transition behavior persists under alternative optimizers, nonlinear conditional quantiles, and loss penalties (C.3–C.5). It adds neural-model comparisons, fixed-budget allocation sensitivity, and feature-distribution diagnostics using histograms, QQ plots, and tail-index estimates (D.2.3–D.4). The heavy-tail evidence is observational rather than a controlled perturbation experiment.

E5.justification: v2 introduces Hill tail-index estimation and a threshold of xi > 0.25 for classifying heavy-tailed features (D.4), adding a statistical estimation procedure. Section 6's averaging over 20 independent trials is unchanged. No increased run count or newly specified confidence-band procedure is reported.

E6.justification: v2 adds results for alternative training choices, nonlinear scenarios, optimizer/model comparisons, and distribution diagnostics. Figure 13 reports cpusmall interval-length elbows near alpha = 0.045 and 0.003. The original Figure 3 fit of -2.24 and Figure 5 slope of 0.92 remain unchanged. The earlier MEPS calibration-fraction plots are replaced by differently organized evaluations, preventing a reliable same-setting performance comparison.

T1.justification: v2 removes v1 Appendix A's argument that variance-reduced optimization yields exponentially decaying quantile-estimation error. The principal bounds and proof chains otherwise remain substantively unchanged. The step size added to Theorem 3.1 was already specified in v1 Corollary B.1, so it clarifies an existing condition rather than introducing a new theoretical regime.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: non-asymptotic CQR/CMR efficiency bounds jointly depending on training size, calibration size, and alpha; phase transitions; and implications for data allocation. The expanded experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: v1 already states an oracle-optimality condition. v2 Section 7 expands this into concrete multimodal/basin-shaped failure cases for interval scores and discusses the costs of relaxing linearity. New interpretations address optimizer volatility, nonlinear/heavy-tailed applicability, and empirical allocation advice. Appendix D.3 also incorrectly associates non-vanishing behavior with alpha = omega(n^-1/2), conflicting with Figure 2's same-order phase diagram.

D1.justification: v2 supplies substantial technical information for its expanded experiments: Gaussian smoothing scale, L1 coefficient 0.001, Huber parameters delta = 0.5 and lambda = 0.1, momentum 0.9 and PyTorch defaults, and neural networks with 10-unit ReLU hidden layers. Table 1 documents dataset dimensions and sample counts. v1's real-data ridge-regression description disappears, without establishing precisely how that earlier implementation changed.

R1.justification: v2 relates its assumptions to Shen et al.'s online quantile regression and credits Bobkov and Ledoux for the retained quantile lemma. It adds references supporting the new optimizers, datasets, penalties, and tail analysis, while removing SAG/SVRG/SAGA references with the deleted discussion. The main positioning against prior conformal-efficiency analyses remains unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 adds an experimental roadmap and a limitations/discussion section, organizes the real-data appendix into dedicated subsections, and shortens bibliographic entries. Existing introductory, methodological, theoretical, and concluding prose is largely retained; the revision is not an extensive rewrite of the established narrative.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with optimizer/model comparison grids, synthetic robustness plots, an allocation figure, feature histograms and QQ plots, and a dataset table. These go beyond relocating existing material. The earlier MEPS plots grouped by calibration fraction are replaced, while Figures 1–5 are largely retained.

improvement.justification: The added optimizer, loss, nonlinear-model, and allocation studies provide useful checks beyond v1's narrow demonstrations, while Section 7 makes applicability limits clearer. These improve empirical support and interpretation. The gains are tempered by proxy oracle lengths, incomplete calibration and uncertainty documentation, and new inconsistencies in Figure 12's dataset caption and Appendix D.3's phase-regime interpretation.
